Title: Ethnic minority representation in UK COVID-19 trials: systematic review and meta-analysis
Snippet: This systematic review of 30 trials with over 100,000 participants shows that Asian, Black and Mixed ethnic groups are either under-represented to a greater extent or incorrectly documented as "BAME", "Other", "non-white" or "Unknown" in UK COVID-19 RCTs. Underrepresentation in clinical trials occur at the system, individual and interpersonal level and require complex solutions, which should be approached at trial conception and considered throughout the research process. Reporting of trials by ethnicity lacks consistency, with obsolete terminology in common use, and grouping of multiple ethnicities commonplace despite genetic and phenotypic differences. Few trials report specific methods for recruiting participants from ethnic minorities. Those conducting trials need to make use of available frameworks for recruiting patients and report data that are consistent in terminology and have greater transparency.

Title: Reporting of Participant Race and Ethnicity from COVID-19 Randomized Controlled Drug and Biologicals Trials: A Scoping Review.
Snippet: Racial and ethnic minorities have been disproportionally burdened by hospitalization and death due to COVID-19. Participation of individuals of diverse races and ethnicities in clinical trials according to study-level characteristics of randomized controlled trials (RCT) that test effectiveness of COVID-19 drugs could be insightful for future researchers. The objective of this scoping review was to describe frequency of race and ethnicity reported as demographic variables and specific reporting of race and ethnicity according to COVID-19 RCT characteristics. We conducted comprehensive searches in Pubmed, ProQuest, WHO Database, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and gray literature via preprint servers from 1/1/2020 to 5/4/2022. We included RCTs on emergency- or conditionally-approved COVID-19 drug interventions (remdesivir, baricitinib, and molnupiravir) with or without comparators. Self-reported race as American Indian/Pacific Islander, Asian, Black/African American, or White, ethnicity as Hispanic/Latinx, study design characteristics, and participant-relevant data were collected. A total of 17 RCTs with 17935 participants was included. Most (n=13, 76%) reported at least one race and ethnicity and were US-based, industry-funded RCTs. Asian, Black, Latinx, and White participants were mostly enrolled in RCTs that studied remdesivir. Native American and Hawaiian participants were mostly assessed for progression to high-flow oxygen/non-invasive ventilation. Time to recovery was assessed predominantly in Black and White participants, while hospitalization or death was mostly assessed in Asian, Latinx, and multi-race participants. Trialists should be aware of RCT-level factors and characteristics that may be associated with low participation of racial and ethnic minorities, which could inform evidence-based interventions to increase minority participation.

Title: Distribution of age, sex, race, and ethnicity in COVID-19 clinical drug trials in the United States: A review
Snippet: Background COVID-19 quickly overwhelmed the world, but disproportionately affects certain communities, particularly minority groups. Despite overrepresentation among COVID-19 cases and death, minority groups were underrepresented in some of the early COVID-19 clinical trials. Objective To assess and compare the demographic characteristics of COVID-19 clinical trial participants to national COVID-19 data. Methods PubMed was searched from December 1, 2019 to November 24, 2020, for randomized controlled trials evaluating a pharmacologic treatment for COVID-19 patients from one or more U.S. sites written in the English language following the PRISMA checklist. Descriptive statistics were calculated to characterize patient demographics enrolled in the included clinical trials, as well as for comparison with national COVID-19 data. Results A total of 4472 records were identified, of which 16 studies were included. The median number of participants was higher in studies of nonhospitalized patients compared to those of hospitalized patients (n = 452 [range 20–1062] vs n = 243 [152–2795]). Ten (63%) studies reported mean or median ages of 50 years or older among all study arms. Males comprised more than half of the study cohort in ten (63%) studies. Race and ethnicity were reported separately in four (25%) studies but were combined when reported in five (31%) studies, while six (38%) reported only race or ethnicity. Proportional representation based on age, sex, race, and ethnicity was evident in some trials, but not in others, when compared to national data. Conclusion Overall, participants often did not reflect the actual population with COVID-19 and demographic characteristics were inconsistently reported.

Title: 460. Disproportionalities in COVID-19 Clinical Drug Trials in the United States: A Systematic Literature Review
Snippet: Abstract Background To combat higher rates of COVID-19 infection, hospitalization, and death among minorities, it is crucial to identify safe, efficacious, and generalizable treatments. Therefore, the purpose of this systematic literature review was to assess the demographic characteristics of COVID-19 clinical trial participants. Methods A literature search was performed according to the PRISMA checklist using PubMed from December 1, 2019 to November 24, 2020 with the following search terms: 2019-nCoV, COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, clinical trial, randomized controlled trial, observational study, and veterinary. To capture additional results, keyword searches were performed using various versions and plural endings with the title/abstract field tag. Randomized controlled trials evaluating a pharmacologic treatment for COVID-19 patients from one or more U.S site written in the English language were eligible for inclusion. Descriptive statistics were calculated to characterize age, gender, race, and ethnicity of patients enrolled in the included COVID-19 clinical trials, as well as for comparison with national COVID-19 data. Results A total of 4472 records were identified, of which 16 were included. Most were placebo-controlled (69%) and included hospitalized patients with COVID-19 (69%). Demographic data were reported for each study arm in 81% of studies. Median number of participants was higher in studies of nonhospitalized patients (n=452 [range 20-1062] vs n=243 [range 152-2795]). Nine (56%) studies reported mean or median ages of 50 years or older amongst all study arms. Males comprised more than half of the study cohort in 50% of studies. Race and ethnicity were reported separately in five (31%) studies, reported in combination in four (25%), while six (38%) reported only race or ethnicity. White or Caucasian patients made up most participants across all arms in 75% of studies. Based on national COVID-19 data, hospitalizations were similar between White persons and African American persons, but higher than other race or ethnic groups, and evenly distributed among males and females. Title: COVID-19 disparities: An urgent call for race reporting and representation in clinical research
Snippet: We observed that, to date, race/ethnicity is not uniformly collected or reported in clinical research studies related to COVID-19 treatments. Among racial/ethnic data we were able to assess, Black patients were consistently underrepresented relative to their disease burden. Given that three of the six studies are retrospective observational research, these data may also suggest that there are disparities in utilization patterns of novel COVID-19 treatments based on race/ethnicity. However future research will need to examine this further. According to the Center for Disease Control, 33.5% of COVID-19 cases in the U.S. were Hispanic and 20.1% were Black [10], despite comprising 18.5% and 13.4% of the population respectively [11]. Given that racial/ethnic disparities in COVID-19 disease burden and outcomes have emerged in the United States, it is essential that all investigators uniformly report race/ethnicity data as well as attempt, in earnest, to obtain representativeness among study participants in order to ensure that we do not develop a further widening of the treatment gap during this pandemic. As of today, there are 221 COVID-19 clinical trials recruiting in the United States [12], it is critical that they aim to achieve representation among participants.

Reporting of trials by ethnicity lacks consistency, with obsolete terminology in common use, and grouping of multiple ethnicities commonplace despite genetic and phenotypic differences. Few trials report specific methods for recruiting participants from ethnic minorities. Those conducting trials need to make use of available frameworks for recruiting patients and report data that are consistent in terminology and have greater transparency.

snippet.text: Racial and ethnic minorities have been disproportionally burdened by hospitalization and death due to COVID-19. Participation of individuals of diverse races and ethnicities in clinical trials according to study-level characteristics of randomized controlled trials (RCT) that test effectiveness of COVID-19 drugs could be insightful for future researchers. The objective of this scoping review was to describe frequency of race and ethnicity reported as demographic variables and specific reporting of race and ethnicity according to COVID-19 RCT characteristics. We conducted comprehensive searches in Pubmed, ProQuest, WHO Database, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and gray literature via preprint servers from 1/1/2020 to 5/4/2022. We included RCTs on emergency- or conditionally-approved COVID-19 drug interventions (remdesivir, baricitinib, and molnupiravir) with or without comparators. Self-reported race as American Indian/Pacific Islander, Asian, Black/African American, or White, ethnicity as Hispanic/Latinx, study design characteristics, and participant-relevant data were collected. A total of 17 RCTs with 17935 participants was included. Most (n=13, 76%) reported at least one race and ethnicity and were US-based, industry-funded RCTs. Asian, Black, Latinx, and White participants were mostly enrolled in RCTs that studied remdesivir. Native American and Hawaiian participants were mostly assessed for progression to high-flow oxygen/non-invasive ventilation. Time to recovery was assessed predominantly in Black and White participants, while hospitalization or death was mostly assessed in Asian, Latinx, and multi-race participants. Trialists should be aware of RCT-level factors and characteristics that may be associated with low participation of racial and ethnic minorities, which could inform evidence-based interventions to increase minority participation.

snippet.text: Background COVID-19 quickly overwhelmed the world, but disproportionately affects certain communities, particularly minority groups. Despite overrepresentation among COVID-19 cases and death, minority groups were underrepresented in some of the early COVID-19 clinical trials. Objective To assess and compare the demographic characteristics of COVID-19 clinical trial participants to national COVID-19 data. Methods PubMed was searched from December 1, 2019 to November 24, 2020, for randomized controlled trials evaluating a pharmacologic treatment for COVID-19 patients from one or more U.S. sites written in the English language following the PRISMA checklist. Descriptive statistics were calculated to characterize patient demographics enrolled in the included clinical trials, as well as for comparison with national COVID-19 data. Results A total of 4472 records were identified, of which 16 studies were included. The median number of participants was higher in studies of nonhospitalized patients compared to those of hospitalized patients (n = 452 [range 20–1062] vs n = 243 [152–2795]). Ten (63%) studies reported mean or median ages of 50 years or older among all study arms. Males comprised more than half of the study cohort in ten (63%) studies. Race and ethnicity were reported separately in four (25%) studies but were combined when reported in five (31%) studies, while six (38%) reported only race or ethnicity. Proportional representation based on age, sex, race, and ethnicity was evident in some trials, but not in others, when compared to national data. Conclusion Overall, participants often did not reflect the actual population with COVID-19 and demographic characteristics were inconsistently reported.

snippet.text: Abstract Background To combat higher rates of COVID-19 infection, hospitalization, and death among minorities, it is crucial to identify safe, efficacious, and generalizable treatments. Therefore, the purpose of this systematic literature review was to assess the demographic characteristics of COVID-19 clinical trial participants. Methods A literature search was performed according to the PRISMA checklist using PubMed from December 1, 2019 to November 24, 2020 with the following search terms: 2019-nCoV, COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, clinical trial, randomized controlled trial, observational study, and veterinary. snippet.text: We observed that, to date, race/ethnicity is not uniformly collected or reported in clinical research studies related to COVID-19 treatments. Among racial/ethnic data we were able to assess, Black patients were consistently underrepresented relative to their disease burden. Given that three of the six studies are retrospective observational research, these data may also suggest that there are disparities in utilization patterns of novel COVID-19 treatments based on race/ethnicity. However future research will need to examine this further. According to the Center for Disease Control, 33.5% of COVID-19 cases in the U.S. were Hispanic and 20.1% were Black [10], despite comprising 18.5% and 13.4% of the population respectively [11]. Given that racial/ethnic disparities in COVID-19 disease burden and outcomes have emerged in the United States, it is essential that all investigators uniformly report race/ethnicity data as well as attempt, in earnest, to obtain representativeness among study participants in order to ensure that we do not develop a further widening of the treatment gap during this pandemic. As of today, there are 221 COVID-19 clinical trials recruiting in the United States [12], it is critical that they aim to achieve representation among participants.

harder.brainstorming: The seed asks for examples of underreporting despite policies, which is straightforward retrieval of documented gaps. Strategies to consider: (1) False premise—claim underreporting is *increasing* when it may be flat/declining, but meta-analyses likely track trends so this is retrievable. (2) Unanswerable temporal specificity—ask about underreporting in a very recent window where systematic reviews don't exist yet, but that's artificial difficulty. (3) Cross-domain reasoning trap—ask which policies are *most* violated, requiring the system to compare compliance rates across different mandates (NIH, FDA, journal policies) when papers rarely make such comparisons directly. (4) Mechanistic explanation requirement—force the system to explain *why* underreporting persists despite policies, moving from 'what examples exist' to 'what causal barriers prevent compliance' which requires synthesizing implicit explanations scattered across discussion sections rather than stated findings. (5) Embedded constraint contradiction—ask for examples where underreporting occurred *in compliance* with policies, exploiting loopholes/exemptions that the system must recognize from fine print rather than headline requirements. Option 4 seems strongest: the literature documents underreporting extensively, but the causal mechanisms (investigator burden, institutional barriers, participant distrust) are typically mentioned tangentially, never assembled into a systematic explanation, requiring genuine synthesis rather than retrieval.
harder.chosen_strategy: Shift from existence proof to causal explanation: require synthesis of WHY underreporting persists (mechanistic barriers) rather than THAT it exists (documented examples).
harder.updated_question: Why does race/ethnicity underreporting persist in research studies despite policies mandating such data collection?
harder.why_harder: The literature extensively documents that underreporting exists and which fields/studies exhibit gaps, making examples easy to retrieve. However, explaining why it persists requires synthesizing causal barriers (investigator burden, lack of enforcement mechanisms, participant refusal, institutional capacity gaps, loophole exploitation) that are mentioned fragmentarily across disparate sources—often buried in discussion sections or editorials—but never assembled into a systematic causal model. A survey-strong system can list compliance failures but struggles to construct the multi-level explanation of persistence.
harder.verification_criterion: The answer must identify at least three distinct mechanistic barriers to compliance cited from its own sources, where each barrier operates at a different level of causation: investigator-level (e.g., perceived irrelevance, collection burden), institutional-level (e.g., lack of enforcement, absent infrastructure), or participant-level (e.g., distrust, refusal to disclose). Fails if it only describes the existence of underreporting gaps, lists policy requirements without explaining non-compliance, or offers speculative barriers not grounded in its cited empirical literature.

attempts.answer:
Summary

Despite federal and institutional mandates to collect race/ethnicity, underreporting and misclassification persist due to a convergence of policy fragmentation, identity complexity, privacy and trust concerns, operational burdens in study workflows, and weak data infrastructure for modern categories and disaggregation. <cite id="ff70810a-0">Inconsistencies in how ethnicity and race are collected and reported are widespread, and a growing share of respondents reject or reject fit into predefined categories, with large numbers selecting “some other race,” especially among Hispanic/Latino populations</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-1">Even with OMB standards, studies still report discrepancies in race/ethnicity recording, with lower concordance between self-report and administrative/EHR data among non-White patients</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">At population surveillance scale, missingness of race/ethnicity remains high despite mandates, requiring new incentives and infrastructure</cite>. Below, we synthesize the key drivers and mitigation strategies.

Policy fragmentation and inconsistent measurement formats

Mandates exist but are implemented through heterogeneous instruments and formats that vary across sectors and data systems, creating friction and ambiguity for respondents and providers. <cite id="ff70810a-1">The OMB standards specify preferred two-step questions (separate race and ethnicity, with the ethnicity question first), yet many studies and datasets use combined or variant formats, which undermines comparability and contributes to errors</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-0">Respondents frequently feel they do not belong in predefined categories; for example, a large share of census respondents choose “some other race,” and many Hispanic mothers select “some other race” on birth certificates, partly due to uncertainty about how to identify or distrust of categories</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">State-level COVID-19 surveillance also shows substantial variation in completeness of racial data and exclusion of multiracial identities when methods don’t allow multiple selections, weakening monitoring for Black, Indigenous, and People of Color</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Methodological guidance emphasizes avoiding crude aggregation of multiple races/ethnicities into residual categories, prioritizing self-identified, disaggregated categories, and standardizing documentation to reduce bias and misclassification</cite>.

Identity complexity, misfit with categories, and cross-source discordance

Race/ethnicity are fluid and context-dependent identities; categorical survey/EHR fields often fail to capture this nuance, leading to omission or strategic vagueness. <cite id="ff70810a-1">Hispanic/Latino populations show particularly large discrepancies between self-report and administrative records, with concordance ranging 39–97% across datasets and misclassification more frequent among non-White patients</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-0">Many people report “some other race” or deliberately vague identities, reflecting misfit with available labels and concerns about stereotyping</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-2">Participants describe ethnicity as “sensitive” and complex, recounting experiences with racial profiling that increase suspicion and lead them to withhold or deliberately obscure ethnicity information, sometimes providing minimally specific labels to reduce risk</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Standard survey formats—close-ended categories with an “other” option, “select all that apply,” and open-ended specification—still incur limitations; improving question wording, language clarity, and involving diverse communities can reduce bias at data collection</cite>.

Privacy, fear of misuse, and distrust

Underreporting is often a privacy-preserving response when participants fear stereotyping, profiling, or misuse—risks amplified by current social contexts and surveillance-heavy environments. <cite id="d1f440dd-1">Forty-two percent of participants chose not to report their ethnicity in a genetic testing context; cited reasons included uncertainty, fear of being wrong, perceived lack of privacy, and concerns about misuse/misinterpretation, especially given histories of problematic race use in research and clinical settings and contemporary racial profiling</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-0">Minoritized ethnic individuals report difficulties disclosing personal information about ethnicity due to its historical and social charge; inconsistent datasets hinder fair auditing, making trust-building, transparent privacy terms, and clear data collection practices essential</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-2">Experiences with racial profiling foster general suspicion and reluctance to share information, extending beyond ethnicity to other identifiers; participants prefer face-to-face disclosure or avoid sharing ethnicity altogether, reflecting distrust of how information may be used by institutions and algorithms</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-3">Privacy-by-design approaches for fairness measurement propose minimizing processed data, avoiding assigning single categories to individuals, enforcing strong security, and offering transparency and opt-out controls to respect sensitivities while enabling needed demographic estimation</cite>.

Operational and workflow barriers in research platforms and consent

Even when mandates exist, study processes can inadvertently discourage reporting, and incentives are often misaligned. <cite id="d1f440dd-3">In platform-based research, completion implies consent and there are no tangible incentives for demographic reporting; for some populations, this lack of incentive and the expectation to self-enroll via generic portals is associated with underrepresentation relative to population benchmarks</cite>. <cite id="9cd445de-3">Online repositories and REDCap-based surveys commonly rely on unsigned preamble consents with implied consent and no tangible incentives, with observed underrepresentation in Hispanic/Latino and Black/African American groups compared to national demographics</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">Missingness is often concentrated in multiracial and Hispanic communities when forms don’t allow multiple identities, and without better data modernization and funding, health departments cannot adequately allocate resources or analyze disparities</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-1">In contexts where ethnicity is optional with little perceived benefit or privacy protections, missingness can reach substantial proportions, and patterns of nonresponse are deliberate rather than absent for income or occupation</cite>.

System infrastructure and incentives gaps

Underreporting persists because infrastructure and incentives do not align to value complete, disaggregated, and up-to-date race/ethnicity data. <cite id="ff70810a-2">COVID-19 case surveillance shows persistent missingness of race/ethnicity across states despite national mandates; variation in completeness, lack of multiracial representation, and joint collection problems weaken surveillance for BIPOC communities and hinder resource allocation</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Recommendations include system-wide protocols for standardized documentation, mapping data to national standards, centralized harmonization, and validation prior to analysis to support disaggregated, self-identified data</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-3">Privacy-preserving estimation frameworks emphasize data minimization, no individual assignment, strong security, and member control with opt-outs, recognizing that fairness monitoring often requires demographic attributes while respecting sensitivities</cite>.

Why mandates alone are insufficient

Mandates create a necessary baseline, but fragmented policies, unclear categories, and lack of alignment between survey/EHR instruments and lived identities create friction at the point of data collection. <cite id="ff70810a-1">Even standardized OMB categories coexist with inconsistent application in research and administrative systems, producing discordant race/ethnicity across sources and undermining disparity analyses</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-0">Respondent identity misfit and the burden of selecting “other” or vague labels are common, especially among Hispanic/Latino populations, and these patterns erode data reliability</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-1">When privacy risks and potential misuse are salient, participants may deliberately omit ethnicity, reflecting a broader risk perception that is not addressed by mandates alone</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">At the system level, missingness and aggregation practices persist without targeted investments, incentives, and modernization, reinforcing underreporting and misclassification</cite>.

Mitigations and promising practices

A multi-pronged approach can reduce underreporting while respecting privacy and identity complexity. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Prioritize self-identification with categories that reflect Indigenous and other conceptualizations of belonging, enable multiple race/ethnicity selection, and implement analytic tools (e.g., NLP) to extract demographic data from unstructured fields</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Adopt system-wide protocols for standardized documentation, enable disaggregation, and validate data before analysis to minimize misclassification</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-3">Use privacy-by-design approaches for demographic estimation (data minimization, no individual category assignment where possible, strong security, transparency, and opt-out controls) to support fairness auditing without exposing sensitive identifiers</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-0">Build trust through transparent privacy terms, co-design with affected communities, and clear communication about how data will be used to avoid discriminatory outcomes</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">Couple mandates with appropriate incentives and funding for public health and research agencies to reward high-quality, complete race/ethnicity reporting and to modernize data systems</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-1">Ensure tangible consent processes with privacy protections and, where data are optional, provide clear benefits and safeguards to reduce perceived risks and increase willingness to report</cite>.

Remaining uncertainties and needed evidence

Two gaps remain. First, platform-specific default opt-out/consent mechanics may suppress reporting, but we lack cross-platform, comparative audits of REDCap and related systems documenting how defaults, implied consent, and lack of incentives affect underreporting by race/ethnicity; prospective evaluations of opt-out-first designs versus explicit consent with privacy-preserving options would clarify effects. Second, longitudinal impacts of “select all that apply” and self-identification on retention and bias require pooled analyses across sectors to confirm that improved categorization does not reduce participation or exacerbate missingness in already-underrepresented groups. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Pooling datasets and testing language/format changes, with community input, is a proposed path to reduce bias, and such studies could quantify reductions in missingness and misclassification</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-2">Surveys that incorporate trust-building and transparent data use may shift opt-out rates, but randomized or quasi-experimental comparisons are needed</cite>.

Practical implications

Researchers and funders should redesign instruments to reflect lived identities, align with OMB standards across systems, and embed privacy-by-design practices with clear opt-out and control mechanisms, while investing in data modernization and community engagement to restore trust and make reporting valuable and safe. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Adopting self-identified, disaggregated categories, standardized documentation protocols, and centralized harmonization can improve completeness and reduce misclassification</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-3">Estimation frameworks that minimize exposure of sensitive attributes and provide member control can enable fairness auditing without increasing reporting burdens or privacy risks</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">Ultimately, without modernization and incentives aligned to the public health and research mission, missingness will continue to obscure disparities and misguide resource allocation</cite>.

Despite federal and institutional mandates to collect race/ethnicity, underreporting and misclassification persist due to a convergence of policy fragmentation, identity complexity, privacy and trust concerns, operational burdens in study workflows, and weak data infrastructure for modern categories and disaggregation. <cite id="ff70810a-0">Inconsistencies in how ethnicity and race are collected and reported are widespread, and a growing share of respondents reject or reject fit into predefined categories, with large numbers selecting “some other race,” especially among Hispanic/Latino populations</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-1">Even with OMB standards, studies still report discrepancies in race/ethnicity recording, with lower concordance between self-report and administrative/EHR data among non-White patients</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">At population surveillance scale, missingness of race/ethnicity remains high despite mandates, requiring new incentives and infrastructure</cite>. Below, we synthesize the key drivers and mitigation strategies.

Policy fragmentation and inconsistent measurement formats

Mandates exist but are implemented through heterogeneous instruments and formats that vary across sectors and data systems, creating friction and ambiguity for respondents and providers. <cite id="ff70810a-1">The OMB standards specify preferred two-step questions (separate race and ethnicity, with the ethnicity question first), yet many studies and datasets use combined or variant formats, which undermines comparability and contributes to errors</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-0">Respondents frequently feel they do not belong in predefined categories; for example, a large share of census respondents choose “some other race,” and many Hispanic mothers select “some other race” on birth certificates, partly due to uncertainty about how to identify or distrust of categories</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">State-level COVID-19 surveillance also shows substantial variation in completeness of racial data and exclusion of multiracial identities when methods don’t allow multiple selections, weakening monitoring for Black, Indigenous, and People of Color</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Methodological guidance emphasizes avoiding crude aggregation of multiple races/ethnicities into residual categories, prioritizing self-identified, disaggregated categories, and standardizing documentation to reduce bias and misclassification</cite>.

Identity complexity, misfit with categories, and cross-source discordance

Race/ethnicity are fluid and context-dependent identities; categorical survey/EHR fields often fail to capture this nuance, leading to omission or strategic vagueness. <cite id="ff70810a-1">Hispanic/Latino populations show particularly large discrepancies between self-report and administrative records, with concordance ranging 39–97% across datasets and misclassification more frequent among non-White patients</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-0">Many people report “some other race” or deliberately vague identities, reflecting misfit with available labels and concerns about stereotyping</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-2">Participants describe ethnicity as “sensitive” and complex, recounting experiences with racial profiling that increase suspicion and lead them to withhold or deliberately obscure ethnicity information, sometimes providing minimally specific labels to reduce risk</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Standard survey formats—close-ended categories with an “other” option, “select all that apply,” and open-ended specification—still incur limitations; improving question wording, language clarity, and involving diverse communities can reduce bias at data collection</cite>.

Privacy, fear of misuse, and distrust

Underreporting is often a privacy-preserving response when participants fear stereotyping, profiling, or misuse—risks amplified by current social contexts and surveillance-heavy environments. <cite id="d1f440dd-1">Forty-two percent of participants chose not to report their ethnicity in a genetic testing context; cited reasons included uncertainty, fear of being wrong, perceived lack of privacy, and concerns about misuse/misinterpretation, especially given histories of problematic race use in research and clinical settings and contemporary racial profiling</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-0">Minoritized ethnic individuals report difficulties disclosing personal information about ethnicity due to its historical and social charge; inconsistent datasets hinder fair auditing, making trust-building, transparent privacy terms, and clear data collection practices essential</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-2">Experiences with racial profiling foster general suspicion and reluctance to share information, extending beyond ethnicity to other identifiers; participants prefer face-to-face disclosure or avoid sharing ethnicity altogether, reflecting distrust of how information may be used by institutions and algorithms</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-3">Privacy-by-design approaches for fairness measurement propose minimizing processed data, avoiding assigning single categories to individuals, enforcing strong security, and offering transparency and opt-out controls to respect sensitivities while enabling needed demographic estimation</cite>.

Operational and workflow barriers in research platforms and consent

Even when mandates exist, study processes can inadvertently discourage reporting, and incentives are often misaligned. <cite id="d1f440dd-3">In platform-based research, completion implies consent and there are no tangible incentives for demographic reporting; for some populations, this lack of incentive and the expectation to self-enroll via generic portals is associated with underrepresentation relative to population benchmarks</cite>. <cite id="9cd445de-3">Online repositories and REDCap-based surveys commonly rely on unsigned preamble consents with implied consent and no tangible incentives, with observed underrepresentation in Hispanic/Latino and Black/African American groups compared to national demographics</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">Missingness is often concentrated in multiracial and Hispanic communities when forms don’t allow multiple identities, and without better data modernization and funding, health departments cannot adequately allocate resources or analyze disparities</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-1">In contexts where ethnicity is optional with little perceived benefit or privacy protections, missingness can reach substantial proportions, and patterns of nonresponse are deliberate rather than absent for income or occupation</cite>.

System infrastructure and incentives gaps

Underreporting persists because infrastructure and incentives do not align to value complete, disaggregated, and up-to-date race/ethnicity data. <cite id="ff70810a-2">COVID-19 case surveillance shows persistent missingness of race/ethnicity across states despite national mandates; variation in completeness, lack of multiracial representation, and joint collection problems weaken surveillance for BIPOC communities and hinder resource allocation</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Recommendations include system-wide protocols for standardized documentation, mapping data to national standards, centralized harmonization, and validation prior to analysis to support disaggregated, self-identified data</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-3">Privacy-preserving estimation frameworks emphasize data minimization, no individual assignment, strong security, and member control with opt-outs, recognizing that fairness monitoring often requires demographic attributes while respecting sensitivities</cite>.

Why mandates alone are insufficient

Mandates create a necessary baseline, but fragmented policies, unclear categories, and lack of alignment between survey/EHR instruments and lived identities create friction at the point of data collection. <cite id="ff70810a-1">Even standardized OMB categories coexist with inconsistent application in research and administrative systems, producing discordant race/ethnicity across sources and undermining disparity analyses</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-0">Respondent identity misfit and the burden of selecting “other” or vague labels are common, especially among Hispanic/Latino populations, and these patterns erode data reliability</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-1">When privacy risks and potential misuse are salient, participants may deliberately omit ethnicity, reflecting a broader risk perception that is not addressed by mandates alone</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">At the system level, missingness and aggregation practices persist without targeted investments, incentives, and modernization, reinforcing underreporting and misclassification</cite>.

Mitigations and promising practices

A multi-pronged approach can reduce underreporting while respecting privacy and identity complexity. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Prioritize self-identification with categories that reflect Indigenous and other conceptualizations of belonging, enable multiple race/ethnicity selection, and implement analytic tools (e.g., NLP) to extract demographic data from unstructured fields</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Adopt system-wide protocols for standardized documentation, enable disaggregation, and validate data before analysis to minimize misclassification</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-3">Use privacy-by-design approaches for demographic estimation (data minimization, no individual category assignment where possible, strong security, transparency, and opt-out controls) to support fairness auditing without exposing sensitive identifiers</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-0">Build trust through transparent privacy terms, co-design with affected communities, and clear communication about how data will be used to avoid discriminatory outcomes</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">Couple mandates with appropriate incentives and funding for public health and research agencies to reward high-quality, complete race/ethnicity reporting and to modernize data systems</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-1">Ensure tangible consent processes with privacy protections and, where data are optional, provide clear benefits and safeguards to reduce perceived risks and increase willingness to report</cite>.

Remaining uncertainties and needed evidence

Two gaps remain. First, platform-specific default opt-out/consent mechanics may suppress reporting, but we lack cross-platform, comparative audits of REDCap and related systems documenting how defaults, implied consent, and lack of incentives affect underreporting by race/ethnicity; prospective evaluations of opt-out-first designs versus explicit consent with privacy-preserving options would clarify effects. Second, longitudinal impacts of “select all that apply” and self-identification on retention and bias require pooled analyses across sectors to confirm that improved categorization does not reduce participation or exacerbate missingness in already-underrepresented groups. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Pooling datasets and testing language/format changes, with community input, is a proposed path to reduce bias, and such studies could quantify reductions in missingness and misclassification</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-2">Surveys that incorporate trust-building and transparent data use may shift opt-out rates, but randomized or quasi-experimental comparisons are needed</cite>.

Practical implications

Researchers and funders should redesign instruments to reflect lived identities, align with OMB standards across systems, and embed privacy-by-design practices with clear opt-out and control mechanisms, while investing in data modernization and community engagement to restore trust and make reporting valuable and safe. <cite id="ff70810a-4">Adopting self-identified, disaggregated categories, standardized documentation protocols, and centralized harmonization can improve completeness and reduce misclassification</cite>. <cite id="d1f440dd-3">Estimation frameworks that minimize exposure of sensitive attributes and provide member control can enable fairness auditing without increasing reporting burdens or privacy risks</cite>. <cite id="ff70810a-2">Ultimately, without modernization and incentives aligned to the public health and research mission, missingness will continue to obscure disparities and misguide resource allocation</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Discrepancies in Race and Ethnicity Documentation: a Potential Barrier in Identifying Racial and Ethnic Disparities
Snippet: Ethnicity and race are complex social constructs that influence personal identity and group social relations. Racial and ethnic identification are fluid and specific to place, time, and context [1,2]. Despite their fluidity, federal ethnic and racial categories serve as the basis to ensure inclusion of minorities in research as well as identify and address health disparities in the US health care system [2]. Inaccurate or inconsistent data stratified by race and ethnicity can impede analysis needed to identify improvements in health care and for the identification of population groups that might be the focus of health interventions to decrease health disparities [3]. A step toward achieving more equitable health care is the systematic collection of accurate data on patient/participant race and ethnicity [4]. In 1977, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) issued race and ethnicity standards that state that both race and ethnicity data need to be collected when developing federal reports [5]. Title: SARS-CoV-2 Testing in North Carolina: Racial, ethnic, and geographic disparities
Snippet: While understanding missingness patterns in race-ethnicity data is interesting in itself and merits further investigation, such questions are beyond the scope of this paper. There is some evidence that even after accounting for missing race and ethnicity data in COVID-19 testing and incidence, disparities between race-ethnicity groups persist (Labgold et al., 2021). Further, missing data on race and ethnicity for COVID-19 surveillance is a persistent problem in the United States, despite national mandates to collect these data (Krieger et al., 2020). Thus, we have chosen to report and describe the patterns based on the data that are available using multiple metrics of testing for comparability across race-ethnicity strata because they provide valuable insights into disparities and raise important questions about testing access for marginalized groups. 

Finally, reporting of negative test results was not mandatory in North Carolina until early July (NCDHHS, 2020a). Thus, the resulting analysis may overestimate the overall and specific racial-ethnic positivity rates while also underestimating per capita testing rates in low-incidence areas. Given that the majority of testing, especially early in the outbreak, was performed at the North Carolina State Laboratory of Public Health and a few larger referral centers and/or private companies with locally developed assays, we believe non-reporting likely represents a small proportion of tests performed.

Title: Recommendations to improve race identification in health records: A rapid scoping review
Snippet: • Prioritize self-identification to ensure accurate and respectful representation. 

• Clarify racial categories to reflect Indigenous conceptualizations of belonging. • Use analytic tools (e.g., natural language processing, data mining) to extract race and sociodemographic data from unstructured EHR fields. 

• Implement system-wide protocols to promote standardized documentation of race. • Implement policy and technical changes to enable data disaggregation. 

• Foster cross-sector collaboration to enhance data breadth. 

• Prioritize recent, self-reported data. 

• Move beyond minimal federal standards for racial categorizations. • Prioritize self-reported race and ethnicity data to enhance data accuracy. 

• Avoid observational methods to reduce misclassification risks. 

• Promote standardized practices across systems to support harmonized data collection. • Promote consistency across health databases by prioritizing standardized, disaggregated, and self-identified race classifications. 

• Adopt race-conscious frameworks to avoid obscuring the experiences of racialized populations. 

• Address differences in how race and ethnicity are defined. • Promote self-reporting and updated race and ethnicity information to promote data completeness and accuracy. 

• Promote transparency and trust in data collection practices. • Ensure demographic data is selfreported by patients to improve the accuracy of information. 

• Standardized documentation of race information. • Mapping race data to national standards to improve consistency and comparability across sources. 

• Implement centralized data harmonization to enhance cross-system analyses. 

• Enhance information through natural language processing and geocoding tools. • Validate race and ethnicity data prior to analysis, especially when examining health outcome associations. 

• Collect self-reported data through multiple sources/interactions to account for the fluidity of racial and ethnic identities. • Ensure transparency in how race data is collected and assigned.

documents.snippet: be able to handle sudden increases in workload that might overwhelm the less flexible capacity of public health workers. 27 However, data modernization initiatives should be coupled with appropriate incentives for state and local health departments to reward adherence to already existing laws mandating the collection of data on race and ethnicity in COVID-19 case surveillance. 19 Our findings highlight a high degree of missingness of data on race and ethnicity in the US case surveillance system, which can enhance our understanding of current challenges of using these data to understand COVID-19's impact on Black, Indigenous, and People of Color. First, our study identified substantial variation in the rate at which states are providing case surveillance with complete racial information to CDC. Second, our study highlights states that have no representation of individuals with multiple racial identities because of the methods by which these states collect data on racial identity. Finally, our study highlights ongoing issues in the simultaneous collection of data on race and ethnicity. These elements weaken effective surveillance of COVID-19 outcomes among Black, Indigenous, and People of Color, especially among multiracial and Hispanic communities. Without access to high-quality data on race and ethnicity, local, state, and federal health departments are unable to adequately allocate scarce public resources and address health disparities. These shortcomings in completeness of data on race and ethnicity require investments into public health infrastructure, including data modernization initiatives, adequate funding of public health staff, and education on the importance of collecting race and ethnicity data to build public health systems that provide a clear picture of disease burden in all communities.

documents.snippet:
While understanding missingness patterns in race-ethnicity data is interesting in itself and merits further investigation, such questions are beyond the scope of this paper. There is some evidence that even after accounting for missing race and ethnicity data in COVID-19 testing and incidence, disparities between race-ethnicity groups persist (Labgold et al., 2021). Further, missing data on race and ethnicity for COVID-19 surveillance is a persistent problem in the United States, despite national mandates to collect these data (Krieger et al., 2020). Thus, we have chosen to report and describe the patterns based on the data that are available using multiple metrics of testing for comparability across race-ethnicity strata because they provide valuable insights into disparities and raise important questions about testing access for marginalized groups. 

Finally, reporting of negative test results was not mandatory in North Carolina until early July (NCDHHS, 2020a). Thus, the resulting analysis may overestimate the overall and specific racial-ethnic positivity rates while also underestimating per capita testing rates in low-incidence areas. Snippet: Our analysis highlights the difficulties many minoritised ethnic individuals encounter when asked for personal information, particularly that related to ethnicity. We recognise the complexity of ethnicity as a data label for its historical, political, and social location, which does not capture the nuances of how people feel and define themselves. There are, of course, well-known risks of stereotypical profiling and bias through proxy discrimination. Yet, if services have inconsistencies across datasets, there are some drawbacks to auditing services and any data-driven methods used to enhance services for fairness. Title: Valuing lived experience and co-design solutions to counter racial inequality in data and algorithmic systems in UK’s digital services
Snippet: Lived experience of racism and poor prior experiences with key services subsequently influenced attitudes towards data privacy and information security. Participant 2 described a general suspicion and reluctance to share information irrespective of which service or institution, based on their experience of racial profiling, principally with police services in both Scotland and England. 

For them, 'sensitive' personal information stemmed beyond ethnicity, to include name, location and even statistics related to energy usage leading them to invest in data privacy tools to block, delete and do-not-track for online activities. They only participated in this research and reluctantly signed a consent form, based on the positive prior interaction with the interviewer, who was a person of colour. 

Their ever conscious awareness for data privacy extended to algorithms and smart energy services with concerns around the 'handing' over of mass personal data for the perceived benefit solely of private companies. 

'Algorithms are created by individuals of a certain persuasion, not byor they're not fair, I'll say that much. I know that for a fact, so I am concerned about algorithmic bias … Much like with the police, I will not disclose anything online. I would much rather go and disclose information face-to-face where I can.' While one recounted the absurdity of being asked for their ethnicity in a credit card application, others saw some benefit for services regarding equality monitoring, while others felt that providing ethnicity or religion information could lead to negative stereotyping that could be delivered by an 'objective' digital system as opposed to a 'human' interaction. 

Some reflected on the complexity of ethnicity labelling, feeling the need to caveat their responses with explanations of being born in the UK or having lived here for most of their lives. While reflecting on responses to ethnicity questions, participant 5 expressed concerns of bias and discrimination, which had some influence in how they answered questions. 

'I avoid sharing ethnicity information when I can, not 100% confident about where my information will be used and shared and if it will be taken in a positive perspective. I just say that I'm Black African Caribbean or Black other so it's a bit purposefully vague.' (Participant 5)

Title: Privacy-Preserving Race/Ethnicity Estimation for Algorithmic Bias Measurement in the U.S
Snippet: This leads us to the central problem we address in this paper: monitoring our AI systems for fairness according to U.S. members' race and ethnicity requires knowledge of those members' race and ethnicity; but platform data on race and ethnicity attributes is severely limited. 

Principles We decided to focus this work on the U.S. Our design principles can be summarized as follows: 

• Impact: Race/ethnicity demographic information must be comprehensive and useful enough to enable equal treatment measurements with respect to race and ethnicity at the aggregate level. 

• Privacy: The measurement test must have privacy by design at its core, including: 

-Data minimization: We must use (or "process") the least amount of personal data needed to achieve our objective and respect the sensitivities members may have around race/ethnicity information, including avoiding LinkedIn "assigning," saving, or disclosing race/ethnicity information. 

-No individual race/ethnicity assignment: We will avoid individual assignment of a single race or ethnicity category to members. 

-Strong Security: We will implement privacy and security protections to prevent unauthorized access (internal or external) to this measurement workflow (e.g. efforts to prevent reassociation of an estimate calculation to an identifiable person) 

-Transparency and Member Control: We must be transparent about the personal data we are using for race/ethnicity measurement tests and provide appropriate controls to members. So, even though a single race/ethnicity will not be assigned to any member, members can opt-out of having their personal data used for the purpose of this race/ethnicity measurement test.

Title: Nonrandom Missingness in Child Race and Ethnicity Records and the US Federal Data Standards: Pooled Analysis of Community-Based Child Health Studies
Snippet: This study pooled and harmonized parent-reported data on children's racial and ethnic identity. Additional research is needed to determine whether distinct patterns emerge when this process is applied to adult populations or to self-reported data from children. Nonetheless, OMB race and ethnicity standards do not differentiate racial or ethnic group definitions or data handling techniques (collection, cleaning, or reporting) based on the age of the population. Therefore, we posit that standard survey formats-a set of close-ended race or ethnicity categories with other race, a "select all that apply" instruction, and an open-ended "please specify" field-incur significant limitations for accurately enumerating race and ethnicity in public health research and surveillance. As a result of identifying specific mechanisms in data collection and reporting, we present 3 hypotheses for future investigation into the overlooked drivers of structural racism in health research. 

First, we hypothesize that when survey questions and response formats change to reduce the stigmatizing, incomplete, inconsistent, or unclear language (including language barriers), respondents are less likely to withhold information or identify as a collective category such as other race. 

[61] Thus, researchers can reduce bias in the data collection stage. With targeted investments by funders, researchers could improve the inclusion of underrepresented groups at the design and input stages. Toward this hypothesis, investigators could systematically test for interlinkages between closeand open-ended responses using our decision-making process (Figure 1) to uncover how aggregate and constrained race and ethnicity categories hide or exclude specific groups. Input from diverse community members must be prioritized during this investigation and when designing race and ethnicity survey questions to prevent additional stigma and bias and build trust with communities [18,62,63]. 

Second, we hypothesize that when crude aggregation of individuals of multiple races or ethnicities into residual categories is avoided, the bias associated with aggregation at the data analysis and presentation stages could be substantially reduced. Researchers could substantially reduce race-related bias by making relevant decisions that better capture the diversity of multiracial participants and examine the specificity of treatment effect differences. Reliance on aggregation as the practical method of planning and implementing public health research ignores minoritized groups and blocks paths for further investigation.

attempts.answer:
Summary
Across biomedical research domains, underreporting of race and ethnicity is common, driven by inconsistent definitions, variable data collection, and gaps in public reporting despite federal and journal mandates. <cite id="8b71e8fc-0">Reviews document large disparities in how populations are labeled in biomedical research, with 100 distinct population labels used in top medical journals and only 4.5% of 995 articles formally defining race/ethnicity and 10.5% reporting methods for assigning those designations</cite>. <cite id="52a26946-0">Decades of policies (since the 1990s) and a 2016 NIH final rule requiring demographic reporting on clinicaltrials.gov have been offset by inconsistent enforcement and compliance, with sponsors and researchers citing resource and privacy constraints</cite>.

Domain-Specific Underreporting Rates

Clinical trials
- Registry-level reporting: <cite id="52a26946-1">Since 2017, the NIH Dissemination Policy requires NIH-funded clinical studies to report race and ethnicity to ClinicalTrials.gov, enabling systematic assessment</cite>. <cite id="52a26946-2">A longitudinal analysis of 58,000+ studies (2000–2024) shows the share of studies failing to report race/ethnicity or both fell from over 50% in 2009 to 17% in 2024; interventional and US-based trials were more likely to report, and observational studies were consistently less likely than interventional trials</cite>. <cite id="52a26946-2">By 2024, over half of studies reported both race and ethnicity (and >75% reported race alone), though Asian and other groups remained underrepresented in international contexts</cite>.
- Trial-level reporting: <cite id="52a26946-3">In a cohort of 20,000+ US-based trials, fewer than 44% reported any race/ethnicity data; among reporting trials, minorities were underrepresented, and industry-funded trials had lower reporting and minority enrollment compared with government-funded trials</cite>. <cite id="52a26946-3">Only 25% of trials reported all five major race/ethnicity groups, starkly contrasting with >99% sex reporting</cite>. <cite id="52a26946-4">In a systematic review of 364 phase 2/3 oncology publications (2012–2022) across four high-impact journals, most did not report American Indian or Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander categories, supporting calls for consistent journal policies and transparent reporting aligned with federal requirements</cite>.
- Representation and definitions: <cite id="52a26946-0">Even when reported, definitions and collection methods vary across studies and countries, contributing to incomplete or non-standardized data; in June 2024 the FDA released guidance to enhance enrollment of underrepresented populations</cite>. <cite id="52a26946-0">Historical analyses show White patients had higher odds of enrollment than Asian, Black/African American, and Hispanic participants in adult acute leukemia trials (ORs 0.75, 0.48, 0.44, all p<0.01)</cite>.

Observational and specialty studies
- Digital/mental health interventions: <cite id="9bb555b4-2">A systematic review of 46 trials of internet-based CBT for depression found race reported in most papers, but only 54% outside the US reported other background demographics beyond race; White participants predominated (74.9%), with limited reporting of Asian (5.8%) and Black (7.6%) participants</cite>.
- Chronic disease management: <cite id="9bb555b4-0">A systematic review of intervention studies in patients with multiple long-term conditions found ethnicity recorded in 67.3% of 407 RCTs but only 9.3% accurately detailed methods for recording and reporting ethnicity; language restrictions without translation or cultural adaptation were common, limiting inclusion of minority groups</cite>. <cite id="9bb555b4-0">A review of cardiovascular RCTs found 56% (140/250) included race/ethnicity reporting, highlighting persistent gaps</cite>.
- Epidemiology journals: <cite id="9bb555b4-3">A systematic review of major epidemiology journals (1995–2018) characterized widespread but poorly conceptualized and operationalized use of race/ethnicity; calls for better measurement and interpretation have persisted, and the field has not “done well” at incorporating these data</cite>.

Genetics, biobanking, and OMICS
- Representation and reporting quality: <cite id="8b71e8fc-3">A systematic review on racial/ethnic disparities in genetic testing for hearing loss emphasizes underrepresentation of broadly defined groups and the need for more information by genetic ancestry, country of origin, or self-identification; while case series precluded some Cochrane domains, the authors note methodological limitations and incomplete data extraction, and they highlight that disproportionate application of new technologies (e.g., NGS) in overrepresented populations risks perpetuating disparities</cite>. <cite id="8b71e8fc-0">Across biomedical research, inconsistent population labeling and lack of formal definitions/standardized methods for race/ethnicity undermine interpretability in genetic and biomedical datasets</cite>.
- Underreporting proxies: <cite id="52a26946-3">Industry funding is associated with lower race/ethnicity reporting and minority enrollment; analogous patterns in genetics/biobanking may reflect similar structural drivers (e.g., funding, data standardization) even when direct race/ethnicity reporting percentages are not uniformly reported</cite>. <cite id="8b71e8fc-0">Only 10.5% of reviewed articles reported methods used to assign race/ethnicity labels, a limitation that plagues genetics studies that rely on self-report, proxy reporting, or ancestry inference without transparent pipelines</cite>.

Policy Compliance Targets vs. Observed Rates

Federal mandates and registry requirements
- NIH/CT.gov baseline and goals: <cite id="52a26946-1">NIH’s 2017 policy requires NIH-funded clinical studies to report race and ethnicity to ClinicalTrials.gov, and since 2024 FDA guidance focuses on enrollment of underrepresented populations</cite>. <cite id="52a26946-0">Despite longstanding NIH policies (since the 1990s), enforcement and compliance have been inconsistent, with sponsors citing accountability/resources and privacy concerns</cite>.
- Measured vs. target gaps:
  - <cite id="52a26946-2">Despite the policy baseline, 17% of studies in 2024 still failed to report race/ethnicity or both (down from over 50% in 2009), indicating a gap between mandate and full compliance across study types and international portfolios</cite>. <cite id="52a26946-2">Observational studies remain less likely than interventional trials to report race/ethnicity, suggesting subgroup categories (e.g., API) may be underrepresented in non-intervention contexts</cite>.
  - <cite id="52a26946-3">Across 20,000+ US trials, fewer than 44% reported any race/ethnicity data, and only 25% reported all five major groups; industry-funded trials had lower reporting and minority representation than government-funded trials</cite>.
  - <cite id="52a26946-4">Oncology publications in high-impact journals commonly omitted API subgroups, reinforcing misalignment with ACA-concordant federal reporting expectations</cite>.
- Definitions/methods: <cite id="52a26946-0">Variations in definitions and collection methods across studies impede consistent reporting and can mask underrepresentation</cite>. <cite id="8b71e8fc-0">Only 4.5% of articles formally defined race/ethnicity and 10.5% reported methods for attribution, contributing to noncomparability and underreporting</cite>.

Journal and field-level standards
- Calls for standardized reporting: <cite id="52a26946-4">Oncology publication findings support calls for consistent journal policies and transparent reporting aligned with federal requirements</cite>. <cite id="9bb555b4-2">In mental health digital interventions, only 54% of non-US studies reported additional background demographics beyond race, indicating that editorial enforcement remains uneven</cite>. <cite id="9bb555b4-3">Epidemiology journals acknowledge persistent conceptual and operational deficiencies, underscoring that policy intent (standards) does not automatically translate to consistent practice</cite>.

Synthesis and Comparisons

Title: Race/ethnicity reporting and representation in US clinical trials: a cohort study
Snippet: In our analysis of two decades of data from over 20,000 USA-based clinical trials registered in ClinicalTrials. gov, we found that fewer than 44% of trials report any race/ethnicity data. Among trials that do report race/ ethnicity, as a group minorities remain underrepresented compared to their US populations, though at the subgroup level median Black enrollment is not statistically below their US population. Even after controlling for other trial features and conducting several sensitivity analyses evaluating alternative encodings of race/ethnicity, we found that industry-funded trials were associated with less race/ethnicity reporting and with lower rates of minority race/ethnicity enrollment compared to US government-funded trials. 

While the increase in race/ethnicity reporting is encouraging, it constitutes a low bar with fewer than 25% of trials reporting enrollment data for all five major race/ethnicity groups, in contrast with rates of sex reporting, which remained above 99% for all study years. 19 Reporting progress is further complicated by the large subset of completed trials (excluded from this analysis) that have not reported any trial results. Decades of research have highlighted the clinical and ethical concerns presented by selective reporting of trial results (despite legal reporting obligations for many trials). 23 ur data showed that smaller trials were less likely to report race/ethnicity data. While this may reflect trialists' assessment of the limited utility of tracking small populations within limited studies, the absence of transparent trial demographics obscures the generalizability of results and weakens the medical community's ability to identify gaps or opportunities for further research. 

Our results suggest the lack of consensus among previous studies that examined race/ethnicity reporting rates (ranging 2-58% in one review 2 ) may stem from a lack of power and/or differences among their sampled populations.
